newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Italy suffers as EMU sentiment turns.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Italy suffers as EMU sentiment turns.

text.p: Speculation over a delay to a single European currency gained speed on Friday, leaving Italian bonds as the main casualty, analysts said.

Much of the recent negative feeling towards European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) stems from Germany, where concerns over meeting the Maastricht criteria combine with doubts about selling Italy as a viable first-round member.
"A delay is clearly being discussed, as there would have to be a scenario set up in advance to deal with that," said Bronwyn Curtis, chief economist at Nomura International in London.
"(Chancellor) Kohl is under pressure, German institutions have cold feet, and the BTP/Bund spread couldn't go much lower without further pro-EMU input," she said.
The Italian markets reacted violently early on Friday after rumours that Germany was about to make a statement about a delay in EMU were exacerbated by a breach in technical support.
Although the Bundesbank and the German finance ministry dismissed the rumour as "ridiculous", traders were adopting a feeling of "there's no smoke without fire."
Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at Cooperative Bank in London said BTPs sunk after they fell through technical support around 129.37.

"Instead of convergence you've got divergence trades and that's what's happening to Italy and Spain. They're going the opposite way," he said. "And that's why Bunds are up, and BTPs are down a point."

March BTP futures were down 1.12 at 128.70 by 1148 GMT, while Bunds were up two basis points at 103.66. The spread between 10-year BTPs and comparable Bunds widened to 185 basis points from 181 at the Thursday close.
Curtis said that in her "risk scenario", which supposes an EMU delay, the spread would widen above 200 basis points by the end of March. If all goes well, she said the spread will dip.
Analysts said there were fears that a delay in the date of the start of EMU from the proposed date of January 1999 could effectively mean a cancellation.
Germany holds its general election in October 1998, and Kohl, Europe's longest serving head of government and seen as the guiding light of EMU, has not yet committed himself to stand.
"We have to face the possibility that Kohl may not be around," said Gerlof de Vry, senior bond strategist at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam.
He said investors would increasingly look to return their investments to the core of Europe, as risks over EMU appeared to heighten.

Bunds, OATs, and also gilts were likely to benefit. Gilts were gaining credence as a shelter from the EMU storm, as investors were prepared to take the risks imposed by the uncertain political future in the UK in exchange for shelter from the machinations of EMU.
However, analysts said the bottom line is that the likelihood of EMU going ahead on time has not changed, but market sentiment has turned against it, which is likely to hold sway in the short term.
De Vry said many investors had still not taken the view that a delay was on the cards, and that the BTP/Bund spread would narrow again.
Curtis said she judged the likelihood of an EMU delay at 45 percent, and the likelihood of it going ahead on time at 55 percent.
"Unless there is an actual implicit delay, which will obviously hit very hard, this fall in BTPs is a buying opportunity," said Curtis. "But it's a very risky one."
